questions.q: What are the five stages a document passes through before it's searchable in a RAG pipeline?
options: Load, clean, split into chunks, embed, upsert
Load, embed, split, clean, delete
Clean, upsert, embed, load, retrieve
Split, load, rank, embed, cache
questions.explain: Every source document is loaded, cleaned of boilerplate, split into chunks, embedded, and upserted into the vector database, in that order.

questions.q: What does recursive chunking do differently from fixed-size chunking?
options: It ignores document structure entirely
It tries a list of separators in order — paragraph, then sentence, then word — before falling back to a harder split
It always produces smaller chunks than fixed-size chunking
It requires an embedding call for every sentence
questions.explain: Recursive chunking respects structure by trying larger structural breaks first and only falling back to a harder split (like splitting mid-word) when a piece still doesn't fit the target size.

questions.q: In the RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter example, what does chunk_overlap=50 do?
options: It discards the last 50 characters of every chunk
It limits the splitter to 50 chunks maximum
It repeats the trailing 50 characters of one chunk at the start of the next chunk
It sets the embedding dimensionality to 50
questions.explain: Overlap repeats a small trailing slice of text at the start of the next chunk so that content spanning a chunk boundary still appears in full in at least one chunk.

questions.q: Why does semantic chunking cost more than recursive chunking?
options: It requires a larger vector database
It needs an embedding call per sentence just to decide where the topic shifts and a split should happen
It can only be used with fixed-size chunks
It doesn't support chunk overlap
questions.explain: Semantic chunking has to embed adjacent sentences to measure the similarity drop between them, which means an extra embedding call for every sentence boundary it evaluates.

questions.q: Why does a chunk need to store a document ID and chunk index, not just its text and vector?
options: Vector databases reject chunks without an ID field
It makes the embedding model run faster
Later steps — like citing a source — depend on knowing exactly which document and position a chunk came from
It reduces the size of the stored vector
questions.explain: Metadata like a document ID, chunk index, and page number is what makes it possible to trace a retrieved chunk back to a specific, citable source later in the pipeline.
